result:
The morning light hits different when you haven't slept. Not better, not worse—just *different*, like tasting a color or hearing a shape. I used to chase insomnia like it was a muse, back when I thought suffering produced art instead of just... more suffering. Now I take the little pills and sleep through the night and wake up ordinary, which is its own kind of miracle.

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her windowsill. Hundreds of them, mismatched, collected from decades of clothing that wore out or was outgrown or belonged to people who died. She'd run her fingers through them while talking on the phone, this soft clinking that meant *someone is here, someone is listening.* I have the jar now. I never add to it, never take from it. Sometimes I just open the lid and smell—metal and dust and something faintly like the lavender sachets she tucked in drawers.

There's a theory I read somewhere that every book you've ever loved exists in your body as actual physical changes to your brain tissue. *Pride and Prejudice* is folded into your temporal lobe. *The Bluest Eye* restructured some neurons in your prefrontal cortex. You're literally made of what you've read. I think about this when I can't remember why I walked into a room, or someone's name, or whether I've already told this story. The books are still there, just... crowded. The library expanded without hiring more staff.

I used to be cruel when I was young. Not dramatically—no playground bullying, no calculated destruction. Just the casual cruelty of someone who hasn't yet understood that other people are *real*, that their interior lives are as vivid and urgent as your own. I'd make jokes at someone's expense and feel clever. I'd disappear from friendships when they required work. I'd listen only to plan my next response. Growing out of this felt less like becoming good and more like recovering from a long illness, one where you slowly realize you've been feverish for years.

The best meal I ever had was a tomato sandwich. August, North Carolina, bread so fresh it was still warm from the bakery down the road. The tomato from a farm stand, still sun-hot, sliced thick enough that you had to open your jaw wide. Mayonnaise, salt, pepper. Nothing else. I was twenty-three and heartbroken in that particular way that only happens when you're twenty-three, where the person who left took with them your entire theory of the future. I sat on a porch and ate this sandwich and cried, and the tomato was so *there*, so completely itself, that for three minutes I forgot to be sad. That's not nothing. That's not nothing at all.

We don't talk enough about the boredom of grief. Everyone expects the tears, the anger, the numbness. But the boredom—weeks where nothing happens, where you go through motions, where you realize you've been staring at a wall for twenty minutes and can't account for the time. Grief as waiting room. Grief as elevator music. You want to be better, want to *perform* healing, but mostly you're just... bored, and bored with being bored, and guilty for being bored when someone is dead.

I have a recurring dream where I'm in a house I almost recognize. There are extra rooms, always, rooms that don't belong, and I spend the dream discovering them. Sometimes they're beautiful—a library with a rolling ladder, a greenhouse full of orchids. Sometimes they're wrong, full of water damage or strange machines or doors that open to brick walls. The house is always mine in the dream, always has been, and I wake up with this ache of having forgotten something important. A therapist once told me houses in dreams represent the self. I didn't go back to her; I didn't want to know what the brick walls meant.

My mother sang to plants. Not in a whimsical way, not performance. She'd be watering the ferns and start humming, something wordless, and the plants did grow well, though I suppose that's correlation, not causation. She stopped after my father died. The plants died too, eventually, and she didn't replace them. I bought her a succulent last year, something hard to kill, and she put it on the windowsill and looked at it with an expression I couldn't read. "Thank you," she said, and didn't hum.

There's a particular shade of blue that appears in the hour before dawn, when the night has loosened its grip but the sun hasn't yet arrived to claim the sky. It's not in the crayon box. It's not on the color wheel. I've tried to photograph it, paint it, describe it, and failed every time. Maybe some things are meant to be temporary witnesses, not evidence. Maybe beauty requires expiration to be beauty at all.

I used to think I'd write something important. Now I think the important thing is to write, to keep making sentences even when they don't add up to anything grand, even when they just circle the same few rooms, touching the same few walls, finding them solid, finding them still there. The house has extra rooms. I haven't found them all yet. Maybe I will, maybe I won't, but the looking matters. The looking is the whole thing, in the end.
